## Hands-on 3 – Reproducing the recorded result {#hands-on-3-reproducing-the-recorded-result .smaller}

::: {.small}
**Task 3**, in your workspace: the file that Multi100 gave the analysts, the model of Table 3 without the unemployment rate, random intercepts for countries and country-rounds.
:::

```{.r}
source("R/spec_tools.R")
have_srd <- fetch_multi100()                 # downloaded once from the OSF and checked
srd <- read.csv(.multi100$path)

m_6u3ll <- lme4::lmer(
  trstprl_r ~ im_conc + happy_r + stflife_r + sclmeet_r + distrust + stfeco_r + hincfel +
    stfhlth_r + stfedu_r + winner + far_right + lrscale + hhinc_std + agea + edulvla + female +
    far_right_share + spr_estat + factor(round) + long_im_his + wgi + GDP +
    (1 | country_round) + (1 | cntry),
  data = srd)
coef(summary(m_6u3ll))["im_conc", ]
```

::: {.fragment .small}
Target: ***t* = `r fmt_num(an("6U3LL", "statistic_recorded"), 3)`**, the value that Multi100 recorded for 6U3LL, with a coefficient of `r fmt_num(an("6U3LL", "b_refit"), 3)` on `r fmt_n(an("6U3LL", "n_refit"))` respondents. Type your *t* in chat and hold it until I say "go".
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
**Browser lab:** the OSF does not let a page on another website read the file, so the lab fits the specification of the course closest to this model on the course data, `fit_spec(ess, items = "available")`: `r fmt_num(curve_analogue$b, 3)` on `r fmt_n(curve_analogue$n)` respondents.
:::

::: notes
Now you work. Open your report at Task 3, or the working script. The download should have happened in the first break; if it did not, the first two lines fetch the file now, twenty-nine megabytes, and check that it is exactly the file that the analysts received. The model is written out for you, so read it as you run it: distrust of parliament on concern and the controls of the paper, the variables that describe countries and rounds, and two random intercepts. It takes some seconds to fit. You should land on a t of forty-six point six two five. When you have it, type it into chat, but do not send it: when I say go, everyone sends at once. In the browser lab the file cannot be fetched, so the lab fits the nearest specification of the course instead. [wait for the numbers in chat]
:::

## The file and the model {#the-file-and-the-model .smaller}

::: {.fs-85}
| Fit | Data | Coefficient |
|:--|:--|--:|
| Random intercepts, the model of 6U3LL | the file of the analysts | `r fmt_num(an("6U3LL", "b_refit"), 3)` |
| An intercept for every country-round instead | the file of the analysts | 0.191 |
| The same specification of the course | the course extract | `r fmt_num(curve_analogue$b, 3)` |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
On one file, the model makes no difference. With one model, the file moves the coefficient by `r fmt_num(an("6U3LL", "b_refit") - curve_analogue$b, 3)`.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The two files code the vote controls differently. The file of the analysts counts a vote for the single party that won the last election as a vote for the government, missing the junior partners of coalitions, and counts voters of several mainstream parties, among them the Dutch liberals, as far right.
:::

::: notes
Here is what that number depends on. The first row is what you just fitted. In the second row the random intercepts are replaced with an intercept for every country-round, the fixed effects that the helpers of the course use, on the same file: the coefficient is the same to the third decimal. In the third row the same specification is fitted to the extract that the course built from the survey files, and it drops to point one seven four. [advance] So with one file, the model makes no difference, and with one model, the file does. [advance] The two files code the vote controls differently. The file of the analysts treats a vote for the single largest party as a vote for the government, which misses coalition partners, and its far-right code catches voters of several mainstream parties. A reproduction tests the file as much as the code.
:::

## Two rebuilds from the ESS {#two-rebuilds-from-the-ess .smaller}

::: {.fs-75}
| Analysis | Coefficient | *t* | Respondents |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| SCORE reproduction osf.io/jp7tr, as published | `r fmt_num(rp("SCORE_jp7tr", "b"), 4)` | `r fmt_num(rp("SCORE_jp7tr", "statistic"), 2)` | `r fmt_n(rp("SCORE_jp7tr", "n"))` |
| The same model on the course extract, without the Italian round 2 | `r fmt_num(rp("course_repro_59", "b"), 4)` | `r fmt_num(rp("course_repro_59", "statistic"), 2)` | `r fmt_n(rp("course_repro_59", "n"))` |
| The reference specification, same respondents | `r fmt_num(rp("course_reference_fe_59", "b"), 4)` | `r fmt_num(rp("course_reference_fe_59", "statistic"), 2)` (clustered, 15 df) | `r fmt_n(rp("course_reference_fe_59", "n"))` |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
SCORE received no data or code from OA, so its reproductions rebuilt the variables from the ESS. It scored the coefficient as reproduced approximately and the sample as not: about 69,000 respondents against the 110,732 of the paper, which does not say how it treated missing answers.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The gap of `r fmt_num(rp("SCORE_jp7tr", "b") - rp("course_repro_59", "b"), 4)` between the two rebuilds lies in the two vote controls: among other differences, the reproduction counts voters of the Dutch liberal party as far right. Respondent by respondent, the two files agree on 99.4% of each vote code.
:::

::: {.src}
cases/trust/data/display_reproduction.csv; the reports of the SCORE reproductions are on the OSF.
:::

::: notes
The file of the analysts was itself a rebuild. SCORE received neither data nor code from OA, so two of its teams rebuilt the variables of the paper from the survey files, and the course did the same. The first row is the focal result of one reproduction, point one seven eight. The second row fits its model to the course extract on exactly its respondents, and lands seven ten-thousandths lower. The third, the reference specification of the course, lands in the same place. [advance] SCORE scored the coefficient as reproduced, but not the sample: the paper reports a hundred and ten thousand respondents in every model, and a model that drops missing answers keeps about seventy thousand. [advance] The tiny gap that remains comes from one coding decision, Dutch liberals counted as far right. Two careful rebuilds part ways over details that no published table shows.
:::
